**Talbot H. Green** (born **Paul Geddes**; August 11, 1810 – July 2, 1889) was an American merchant and politician during the mid-19th century, who was exposed as Paul Geddes, an absconder and [embezzler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Embezzlement "Embezzlement") of funds from a [Philadelphia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia "Philadelphia") bank. Born in Pennsylvania to an influential family of Scottish descent, Geddes initially worked in merchandising and engineering. His early career in [Philadelphia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia "Philadelphia") ended abruptly after financial mismanagement and embezzlement led him to leave his wife and four children, flee westward, and adopt the alias Talbot H. Green.

In 1841, Green joined the [Bartleson–Bidwell Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bartleson%E2%80%93Bidwell_Party "Bartleson–Bidwell Party"), a pioneering group of emigrants heading to California. Known for his friendly demeanor and leadership skills, he quickly established himself in the Californian business community. Green worked closely with [Thomas O. Larkin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_O._Larkin "Thomas O. Larkin"), a prominent merchant in [Monterey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monterey,_California "Monterey, California"), and became a key figure in Larkin's mercantile operations.

Green's influence extended beyond business; he played an active role in California's early political and social life. He was a founding member of the [Society of California Pioneers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Society_of_California_Pioneers "Society of California Pioneers"), served on San Francisco's first city council, and participated in significant land transactions. His contributions during the [U.S. military conquest of California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexican%E2%80%93American_War "Mexican–American War") included supplying goods to American forces.

In 1851, rumors of Green's true identity as Paul Geddes surfaced, leading to his departure from California. He relocated to Texas and later worked as a clerk for the secretary of the [United States Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate "United States Senate"). Green spent his final years in [Lewisburg, Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lewisburg,_Pennsylvania "Lewisburg, Pennsylvania"), where he lived quietly until his death in 1889, respected by his community but marked by his earlier misdeeds.

## Early life and career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Talbot_H._Green&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and career")]

Paul Geddes was born on August 11, 1810.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talbot_H._Green#cite_note-3) The Geddes family, of Scottish origin, traces its descent from Paul Geddes, born in Scotland between 1660 and 1670.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talbot_H._Green#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHussey193941-4) The earlier Paul Geddes resided for a time in Ireland, near [Randallstown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randallstown "Randallstown"), County Antrim, where his son James was born in 1704. James Geddes, his wife Margaret Muir, and their three sons, Paul, William, and Samuel, emigrated to America in August 1752, settling in what is now [Dauphin County, Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dauphin_County,_Pennsylvania "Dauphin County, Pennsylvania"). James's sons became prominent locally, with at least one active in the [American Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Revolution "American Revolution"). Samuel Geddes, the youngest son, died in 1788, leaving four children. His second child, James Geddes (1781–1867), was the father of Paul Geddes, later known as Talbot H. Green. James Geddes married his cousin, Mary Geddes (1781–1874), on February 12, 1807, and lived in [Lewisburg, Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lewisburg,_Pennsylvania "Lewisburg, Pennsylvania"), where he was known for his character and integrity, serving as treasurer of a corporation for over forty years.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talbot_H._Green#cite_note-5) He and his wife were [Presbyterians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterian_Church "Presbyterian Church") and raised their three children, Paul, Margaret, and James, in this faith.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talbot_H._Green#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHussey193941-4)

Paul left school early to work in a store for four years and later worked as an assistant engineer on the canal for two years. His father then provided him with $3,000[[b]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talbot_H._Green#cite_note-7) to start a merchandising business. They eventually bought another store in a neighboring town. On February 21, 1832, Paul Geddes was married to Henrietta Fredrick. After their marriage, Paul Geddes and his wife moved to a neighboring town where they established a new branch store. In this town, Geddes took on another business partner and was known as a respected and trusted businessman.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talbot_H._Green#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHussey193942-8)

## Embezzlement

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Talbot_H._Green&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Embezzlement")]

In the spring of 1840, Paul Geddes traveled to [Philadelphia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia "Philadelphia") to buy goods and had a large quantity of wheat consigned to a trading house there. He withdrew $3,000 on account of the wheat but lost the money after a night of drinking. That afternoon, the cashier of the Farmers & Merchants Bank of Philadelphia asked him to carry $105,000[[c]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talbot_H._Green#cite_note-9) to the [Northumberland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northumberland,_PA "Northumberland, PA") bank. Green committed a fraud and stole the money. There is no official record of the exact amount of money Green stole. The incident was described by Green in his letter to [Thomas O. Larkin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_O._Larkin "Thomas O. Larkin"):

> ...They got a carpet bag and put up 105,000$ in it in my presence and sent a porter with me to the hotel. I put it in my trunk and went out. On my return I found that I had been robbed of my money. I was under the excitement of liquor (no excuse) and was, in fact, not myself. I opened the carpet bag and took out nearly 8000$[[d]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talbot_H._Green#cite_note-10) and done the parcel up again. I then went to bed. In the morning [...] I then took the carpet bag to a merchant and told him what it contained and wished him to keep it until next day. The next day I went and paid a good many of my debts with the money and sent some 3000$ to my partner to pay notes we owed in the bank; and that night I left Philadelphia with 375$ determined that my people should never hear of me again. I went West and fell in with the emigration for California...[_[sic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sic "Sic")_][[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talbot_H._Green#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHussey193942-8)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talbot_H._Green#cite_note-FOOTNOTELarkin1850269volume_VIII-11)

Paul Geddes left Pennsylvania, abandoning his wife and four children. He traveled to [New Orleans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Orleans "New Orleans") by ship from [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City"). From New Orleans, he continued his journey by steamboat up the [Mississippi River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi_River "Mississippi River").

## Escape to the West

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Talbot_H._Green&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Escape to the West")]

On board the boat Geddes met an Englishman, Talbot H. Green, who fell ill and died. In gratitude for Geddes's care, the Englishman left him his name and some papers, which he believed might be valuable in the future. Geddes took the name Talbot H. Green and kept the papers. Green continued from [St. Louis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Louis "St. Louis") up the [Missouri River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missouri_River "Missouri River") until he reached [Westport, Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westport,_Kansas_City,_Missouri "Westport, Kansas City, Missouri"), which served as a departure point for the western plains.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talbot_H._Green#cite_note-FOOTNOTELeek2017part_3-12)

In 1841, Green joined the [Bartleson–Bidwell Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bartleson%E2%80%93Bidwell_Party "Bartleson–Bidwell Party"), a group of emigrants heading to California. The group gathered near the [Kansas River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_River "Kansas River") in the spring, with Green, who was in his early thirties at the time. Known for his friendly and cultured demeanor, Green, "of evident culture and very pleasant address," quickly became well-liked by his fellow travelers. On May 18, during a meeting to organize the party, he was chosen to lead the gathering, highlighting his early leadership within the group.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talbot_H._Green#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHussey193933-13)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talbot_H._Green#cite_note-14)

Although Green initially held a prominent role, his influence did not continue during the rest of the journey. As the group moved westward, Green traveled as a regular member of the party. He joined the mess of John Bartleson, the party's captain, along with Charles Hopper, a well-known bear hunter; Gwynn Patton; Nicholas Dawson; and Grove C. Cook, a young man known for his likable but unruly nature, with whom Green developed a close friendship.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talbot_H._Green#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHussey193933-13)

Green carried a case of medicines and earned the title of "doctor" by attending to the sick. He did not stand out from his companions during the journey, and mentions of him by chroniclers are due to his later notoriety rather than his actions on the trek. His fellow travelers later emphasized his presence, influenced by his future reputation.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talbot_H._Green#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHussey193933-13)

Nicholas Dawson noted that Green's most valued possession was a quantity of lead. On the western slope of the [Sierra Nevada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sierra_Nevada "Sierra Nevada") range, the load became too heavy for the pack animal, so Green and Grove Cook hid the lead in a gulch. After reaching [John Marsh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Marsh_(pioneer) "John Marsh (pioneer)")'s ranch near [Mount Diablo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Diablo "Mount Diablo"), Green hired an Indian guide and, with Cook, retrieved the hidden pack. A year later in [Monterey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monterey,_California "Monterey, California"), Dawson met Green again, now wealthy with plenty of cash. Dawson was surprised by Green's sudden wealth, suggesting that the "lead" was actually a more precious metal.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talbot_H._Green#cite_note-FOOTNOTELeek2017part_3-12)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talbot_H._Green#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDawson19339%E2%80%9310,_25,_28,_45,_84-15)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talbot_H._Green#cite_note-16)

## In California

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Talbot_H._Green&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: In California")]

### Business establishment in Monterey

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Talbot_H._Green&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Business establishment in Monterey")]

Green quickly established himself in California's business and social circles. Using John Marsh's bond, dated November 13, 1841, as security for his good behavior, Green moved to [Monterey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monterey,_California "Monterey, California") and began working for [Thomas O. Larkin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_O._Larkin "Thomas O. Larkin"), the town's largest merchant, as a clerk and agent.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talbot_H._Green#cite_note-17) Green soon earned the confidence of his new employer, and by the summer of 1842, he was sent out into the countryside to sell merchandise and conduct general trading. In July of that year, he wrote back to Larkin from [Gilroy's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gilroy,_California "Gilroy, California") rancho, reporting on his business activities. He mentioned, "I find some difficulty in getting along, on account of not speaking the language." A few days later, he wrote again, urging Larkin to come in person as many of the rancheros "would trade with you that won't with me."[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talbot_H._Green#cite_note-FOOTNOTELarkin1850286-18)[[e]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talbot_H._Green#cite_note-20)

Continued trading helped Green become familiar with Californian customs, and his genial personality and open-hearted manners made him very successful in business. Larkin had so much confidence in him that, in May of the next year, he put Green in charge of all the goods in his Monterey store and warehouse, worth a total of $4,292. Green was to manage Larkin's Monterey business for a year, collecting debts, conducting trade, and overseeing his interests. For these services, he was to receive $400 and five percent of the profits.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talbot_H._Green#cite_note-FOOTNOTELarkin185015-21)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talbot_H._Green#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHussey193934-22) Later that month, Larkin gave Green $2,500 in cash to take to Los Angeles, where he was to collect a debt of $500 and offer the total amount to the Governor of the province as a loan. In November 1843, Larkin showed even more trust in Green's honesty and ability by putting him in charge of all his "outdoor business" when he left for a voyage to [Mazatlan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mazatlan "Mazatlan"). This included overseeing his corral, house, garden, sheds, and warehouses.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talbot_H._Green#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHussey193934-22)

On January 1, 1844, Green was tasked with taking an "exact inventory" of all of Larkin's property except his private house. During Larkin's absence, Green was also responsible for ensuring that Mrs. Larkin had sufficient funds and that the servants behaved properly.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talbot_H._Green#cite_note-FOOTNOTELarkin185059volume_I-23) Over the next few years, Green continued working for Larkin, steadily increasing his prestige and standing in the community. In January 1846, he made a contract to manage Larkin's mercantile business, handling goods valued at $10,000 for a period of three years, for one-third of the profits.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talbot_H._Green#cite_note-FOOTNOTELarkin18501volume_IV-24)

### Government role

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Talbot_H._Green&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Government role")]

When the United States [took over California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conquest_of_California "Conquest of California") in July 1846, Green benefited from this event. Acting as Larkin's agent, he supplied a significant portion of the goods purchased by the United States military and naval forces at Monterey in 1846 and 1847. He provided clothing, ordnance, and foodstuffs to figures like [Fremont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_C._Fr%C3%A9mont "John C. Frémont"), Fauntleroy, and [Maddox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_A._T._Maddox "William A. T. Maddox").[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talbot_H._Green#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHussey193935-25)

In the late summer of 1846, Green was appointed to a government office. Captain [William Mervine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Mervine "William Mervine") of the [United States Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Navy "United States Navy") temporarily assigned him as the collector of the port of Monterey. On September 17, Larkin wrote to Commodore [Robert F. Stockton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_F._Stockton "Robert F. Stockton"), recommending that Green be given the office permanently. Likely due to this recommendation, Stockton appointed Green to the position, which he held at a salary of $1,000 a year until October 1847, when President [Polk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_K._Polk "James K. Polk") ordered that customs in captured ports be collected by Army and Navy officers. During Green's appointment, [Walter Colton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Colton "Walter Colton") described him as a native of Pennsylvania who "enjoys a wide reputation for business habits and sterling integrity of character."[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talbot_H._Green#cite_note-FOOTNOTELarkin1850284volume_IV-26)

Green was chosen to sit on the first jury ever summoned in California. Meeting on September 4, 1846, this jury, in the case of [Isaac Graham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isaac_Graham "Isaac Graham") vs. Charles Roussillon, delivered the well-known "enlightened and impartial verdict" to which "both parties bowed without a dissenting word."[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talbot_H._Green#cite_note-27)

There are indications that Green's conduct during the military occupation of California was questionable. In 1848, Lieutenant William A. T. Maddox accused Green in a letter to Larkin of [making false statements](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Making_false_statements "Making false statements") about payments for supplies furnished to the naval forces. Green was evidently able to explain the charges satisfactorily, as Larkin's respect for him did not diminish. In later years, Green admitted to dishonorable conduct and bribery related to the condemnation and sale of the merchant ship _Admittance_ by the [Admiralty Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Admiralty_Court "Admiralty Court") at Monterey and Mazatlan. However, this transaction was not widely known until Green disclosed it.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talbot_H._Green#cite_note-FOOTNOTELarkin1856volume_IX-28)

### Moving to San Francisco

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Talbot_H._Green&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Moving to San Francisco")]

In 1847 and 1848, Green was involved in various business ventures. He traveled to Mazatlan, was in San Francisco in January 1848 selling goods, went to [Benicia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benicia,_California "Benicia, California") in March to address construction matters for Larkin, and visited the gold mines in the fall. During these two years, his focus shifted from Monterey to San Francisco, especially after the discovery of gold, when he anticipated that San Francisco would soon expand significantly.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talbot_H._Green#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHussey193936-29)

Green had owned property in San Francisco for some time, but his significant involvement in the town's business life began on January 1, 1849, when he joined the prominent trading firm of Mellus & Howard. With [William D. M. Howard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_D._M._Howard "William D. M. Howard"), [Henry Mellus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Mellus "Henry Mellus"), and [Francis Mellus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_Mellus "Francis Mellus") as partners,[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talbot_H._Green#cite_note-FOOTNOTELeek2017part_1-30) Green started a career that made him a well-known figure in northern California. Over the course of two years, the firm's name and membership changed several times, but it remained one of the largest in the city. [Samuel Brannan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Brannan "Samuel Brannan") was also involved in several business ventures with the firm. By early 1851, the Mellus brothers had sold their interests in the firm, which continued as a partnership between Green and W. D. M. Howard, under the name Howard & Green.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talbot_H._Green#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDavis1929211,_213,_226-31)

### Green's popularity

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Talbot_H._Green&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Green's popularity")]

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d8/Sir%2C_I_have_been_instructed_by_the_Society_of_California_Pioneers%2C_to_notify_you_that_the_Society_has_been_fully_organized_under_the_Constitution%2C_by_the_election_of_the_following_Officers%2C_viz-_-_%2811422417824%29.jpg/250px-thumbnail.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Sir,_I_have_been_instructed_by_the_Society_of_California_Pioneers,_to_notify_you_that_the_Society_has_been_fully_organized_under_the_Constitution,_by_the_election_of_the_following_Officers,_viz-_-_(11422417824).jpg)

Society of California Pioneers membership certificate. Talbot H. Green is a treasurer.

Green was a popular figure in California with one author claiming, "the widow or the orphan ever found in him a generous friend."[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talbot_H._Green#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite1881124-32) One acquaintance described him as "just about the all-around best man I had ever known."[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talbot_H._Green#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDawson193384-33) Along with his business success, Green gained social prominence and was well known on [the streets of San Francisco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Streets_of_San_Francisco "The Streets of San Francisco"). Despite his plain appearance, his "kind and off-hand" manner, common sense, and fine judgment made him welcome everywhere. According to another acquaintance, "He was respected by all."[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talbot_H._Green#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite1881124-32) In business disputes, Green was often chosen as an arbitrator, frequently serving as the sole arbitrator, even in cases involving large sums. One friend noted, "I cannot recall an instance where his decision was disputed or appealed from by either party."[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talbot_H._Green#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite1881124%E2%80%93125-34)

Prominent figures such as W. D. M. Howard, [Samuel Brannan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Brannan "Samuel Brannan"), [Thomas O. Larkin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_O._Larkin "Thomas O. Larkin"), and [Captain Folsom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Libbey_Folsom "Joseph Libbey Folsom") acknowledged their close personal friendship with Green. In 1851, Howard, Brannan, and Green all lived in similar cottages on the same block of [Mission Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mission_Street "Mission Street"), between [Third](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Street_(San_Francisco) "Third Street (San Francisco)") and Fourth streets.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talbot_H._Green#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHussey193936-29) Green was elected as the first treasurer of the [Society of California Pioneers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Society_of_California_Pioneers "Society of California Pioneers") upon its founding in 1850.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talbot_H._Green#cite_note-35)

In the summer of 1849, a gold-seeker who knew Green described him as "the most popular man of all the old Californians." He noted that Green would have likely been elected as one of California's first senators "had he listened to the entreaties of friends, and allowed his name to be used."[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talbot_H._Green#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite1881125-36) On October 25, 1849, Green married [Sarah Montgomery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarah_Wallis "Sarah Wallis"),[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talbot_H._Green#cite_note-37) the widow of Allen Montgomery, at the [San Jose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Jose,_California "San Jose, California") home of his old friend, Grove C. Cook. The event was noted by the editor of the San Francisco _[Daily Alta California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daily\_Alta\_California "Daily Alta California")_.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talbot_H._Green#cite_note-38)

### Public affairs

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Talbot_H._Green&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Public affairs")]

Soon after his arrival in San Francisco, Green became actively involved in public affairs.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talbot_H._Green#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHittell1898390volume_III-39) On February 21, 1849, he was elected to the San Francisco district Legislative Assembly. When that body was replaced by the [Ayuntamiento (City Council)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ayuntamiento "Ayuntamiento"), he was elected to the Council in August 1849.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talbot_H._Green#cite_note-40) He was re-elected as councilman on January 8, 1850, and served until May of that year.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talbot_H._Green#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHussey193937-41)

As a city official, Green actively participated in civic affairs. He served on the finance committee of the Council and chaired the committee for fencing [Portsmouth Square](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portsmouth_Square "Portsmouth Square").[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talbot_H._Green#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHussey193937-41) Early in 1850, Green and Samuel Brannan were among the councilmen accused of using their positions to secure titles to city property. Records indicate that Green purchased thirty-four lots at sales of town lots in 1849 and 1850. These accusations resulted in a public dispute involving Green.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talbot_H._Green#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHittell1898389%E2%80%93392volume_III-42)

Reports suggest that Green might have been elected [mayor of San Francisco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayor_of_San_Francisco "Mayor of San Francisco") in 1850 if he had not declined to run, allowing [John W. Geary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_W._Geary "John W. Geary") to win the office. Green sought the Democratic nomination for mayor in April 1851.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talbot_H._Green#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite1881125-36) His involvement in this contest ultimately led to his downfall.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talbot_H._Green#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHussey193937-41)

### Exposure and scandal

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Talbot_H._Green&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Exposure and scandal")]

Rumors began circulating in San Francisco that Talbot H. Green was actually Paul Geddes, a man who had absconded with funds from a Pennsylvania bank and left a deserted wife and family. The exact time when these rumors started is unclear. Some sources suggest that a woman recognized him during the celebrations for California's admission into the Union in 1850.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talbot_H._Green#cite_note-FOOTNOTELeek2017part_1-30) Others claim that a woman publicly accused him of being Paul Geddes at a ball, while still others state that a lawyer from [Philadelphia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia "Philadelphia") identified him on the street. Upon being recognized, Green reportedly turned pale, trembled, but firmly denied the accusation.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talbot_H._Green#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite1881126-43)[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talbot_H._Green#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDawson193385-44)[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talbot_H._Green#cite_note-pioneer-45)

Prior to the mayoralty campaign of 1851, rumors about Green being Paul Geddes did not gain enough traction to harm his reputation significantly. However, his entry into the political contest brought these rumors to the forefront. A day or two before the candidates were to be announced, an incident led Green to withdraw his candidacy. Reports vary on the exact nature of the incident: [William Heath Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Heath_Davis "William Heath Davis") suggested that H. P. Hepburn from Philadelphia confronted Green on [Montgomery Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montgomery_Street "Montgomery Street") and accused him of being Geddes in front of friends, while William White indicated that the exposure resulted from a newspaper notice.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talbot_H._Green#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite1881126%E2%80%93128-46)[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talbot_H._Green#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDavis1929226%E2%80%93227-47)[[f]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talbot_H._Green#cite_note-49)

News of the event quickly spread through the city. Green's closest friends visited him to inquire about the truth of the charges, assuring him of their continued friendship and their determination to support him despite any past misdeeds. Green firmly insisted that the case was one of mistaken identity. Realizing that verbal denials would not clear him of suspicion, he offered to return East to resolve the matter and prove his innocence. Within a day or two, he dissolved his partnership with Howard, transferred some of his property to his wife, and settled his affairs as best he could.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talbot_H._Green#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHussey193938-50)

On the afternoon of April 15, 1851, Green left San Francisco on the steamer _[Panama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SS\_Panama "SS Panama")_. His friends stood by him until his departure. Just before he left for the boat, many prominent citizens, merchants, bankers, and others gathered at the Eagle Saloon to bid him farewell, as reported by the next day's [Alta California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alta_California "Alta California"). When the room was filled to capacity, champagne was opened, and Thomas O. Larkin proposed a toast: "The health and prosperity of our friend and fellow citizen, Talbot H. Green; may the best among us be as worthy as we believe him to be." Green responded briefly, thanking everyone for their support and promising to return soon.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talbot_H._Green#cite_note-51) A witness reported that Green broke down and "sobbed." The entire company then formed a procession and escorted him on board the steamer, continuing to shake his hand until the boat departed from the wharf. One of the attendees stated, "We all turned away with a sad, sickening feeling, as the conviction grew that Green was... Geddes."[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talbot_H._Green#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite1881128%E2%80%93129-52)

After several months, there was no news from Green. Reports occasionally stated that he had been seen in the East, but there were no indications that he had attempted to clear his name. Over time, it was accepted that Talbot H. Green was Paul Geddes, who had left his home in the East, leaving behind a wife and four children.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talbot_H._Green#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHussey193939-53)

## Struggles to recover

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Talbot_H._Green&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Struggles to recover")]

Two years later, [Thomas O. Larkin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_O._Larkin "Thomas O. Larkin") received a letter from Talbot H. Green, revealing that Green was indeed Paul Geddes. Green admitted to deceiving his California friends and acknowledged his dishonorable actions. Despite his feelings of betrayal, Larkin decided to support his former clerk and agent. Green, hiding in Tennessee, wrote several desperate letters to Larkin, seeking financial assistance and expressing his remorse.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talbot_H._Green#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHussey193939-53) Green described his hardships and financial struggles, having lost $3,200 and being left penniless. He requested drafts from Larkin to sustain himself.[[g]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talbot_H._Green#cite_note-54) In one of his letters, Green admitted to taking liquor excessively and promised to abstain from it in the future. He expressed a desire to make amends and clear his debts.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talbot_H._Green#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHussey193943-55) Larkin sent Green a draft for $200 in December 1853, which lifted Green's spirits temporarily. Green detailed his early life and the circumstances that led him to adopt the name Talbot H. Green. He explained how he had fled westward, joining the emigration to California with little money.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talbot_H._Green#cite_note-FOOTNOTELarkin1850269volume_VIII-11)

Throughout early 1854, Green continued to receive newspapers and pamphlets from Larkin but no additional funds. He wrote letters describing his dire situation and the need for financial support to clear his debts and return to California. Green's correspondence revealed his growing despair and frustration with his circumstances.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talbot_H._Green#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHussey193945-56) In January 1854, Green received Sarah's application for a divorce, which deeply affected him.[[h]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talbot_H._Green#cite_note-note1-58) He expressed his continued love for her and concern for their child.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talbot_H._Green#cite_note-FOOTNOTELarkin185654volume_IX-59) Despite his financial struggles, Green managed to survive by working and relying on the kindness of others.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talbot_H._Green#cite_note-FOOTNOTELarkin185667volume_IX-60)

By mid-1854, Green's letters indicated increasing distrust of his former associates, William D. M. Howard and Joseph P. Thompson. He detailed his grievances and the financial disputes he had with them. Green's health began to suffer due to the stress and anxiety caused by his uncertain situation.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talbot_H._Green#cite_note-FOOTNOTELarkin1856133volume_IX-61) In late 1854, Green learned that Sarah had remarried, which further devastated him. Despite this, he expressed his hope for her happiness and continued concern for their child. Green struggled with the reality of his situation and the loss of his former life.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talbot_H._Green#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHussey193949-62)

In early 1855, friends and former associates, including [Samuel Brannan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Brannan "Samuel Brannan") and William D. M. Howard, began to take steps to help Green settle his affairs. [Ebenezer Childs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ebenezer_Childs "Ebenezer Childs") played a crucial role in facilitating communication between Green and his benefactors.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talbot_H._Green#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHussey193954-63) Green was eventually able to meet with Brannan in New York City, where arrangements were made to resolve his financial issues.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talbot_H._Green#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHussey193955-64) By March 1855, Green successfully settled his accounts with Howard and planned to return to California. He expressed gratitude for the support from his friends and the hope of starting anew. However, upon his return to California, Green found it difficult to reintegrate into society. He faced awkward and strained interactions with former acquaintances, leading him to seek refuge in the [Sacramento Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sacramento_Valley "Sacramento Valley").[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talbot_H._Green#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite1881130-65)[[i]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talbot_H._Green#cite_note-66)

In January 1856, Green learned of Howard's death,[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talbot_H._Green#cite_note-67) which saddened him.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talbot_H._Green#cite_note-FOOTNOTELarkin1856414volume_IX-68) Green eventually decided to leave California and return to his family in Pennsylvania. In his farewell letter to Larkin, Green expressed his gratitude for the kindness and support he received and his intention to write from the East.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talbot_H._Green#cite_note-FOOTNOTELarkin1856534volume_IX-69)

## Return to Pennsylvania

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Talbot_H._Green&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Return to Pennsylvania")]

In October 1856, Green returned to Pennsylvania and reunited with his wife and family. He observed the unchanged state of his parents and household but found it challenging to reacquaint himself with his own children. Despite the warm reception from former acquaintances, Green felt a sense of emptiness and decided to travel westward with his wife.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talbot_H._Green#cite_note-FOOTNOTELarkin1856566volume_IX-70)

After leaving Pennsylvania, Green was next heard of in Texas, where he was engaged in land speculation under his true name, Paul Geddes.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talbot_H._Green#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite1881130-65) He later lost most of his money and took a position as a clerk to the secretary of the [United States Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate "United States Senate"). In this capacity, he visited California in 1876 and held the office until at least 1878.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talbot_H._Green#cite_note-pioneer-45)

By 1880, Green returned to his boyhood home in [Lewisburg, Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lewisburg,_Pennsylvania "Lewisburg, Pennsylvania"). He spent the remainder of his life there, reportedly enjoying the confidence and respect of the community.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talbot_H._Green#cite_note-pa_records-71) Green never discussed his experiences in California. He died on July 2, 1889, and was survived by his wife and two children.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talbot_H._Green#cite_note-pa_records-71)

## Personal life and family

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Talbot_H._Green&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Personal life and family")]

Those who knew Green described him as a short, square-built man with plain but kindly features. He was "well-known and well-liked".[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talbot_H._Green#cite_note-FOOTNOTELeek2017part_2-72) As Paul Geddes, he married Henrietta Fredrick Geddes. They had children James F. Geddes (1832–1840), Harriet Jenkins Geddes (1835–1855), Mary Elizabeth Geddes (1837–1921), and William Cameron Geddes (1839–1890).

As Talbot H. Green, he married Sarah Armstrong Montgomery (1825–1905), after a lengthy courtship, on October 25, 1849. She divorced him in January 1854.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talbot_H._Green#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHussey193936%E2%80%9337,_45-73) They had a son who was later adopted by Sarah's third husband, Joseph S. Wallis, and took his name to become Talbot H. Wallis.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talbot_H._Green#cite_note-74)

## Legacy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Talbot_H._Green&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Legacy")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c0/GreenSt_plaque_1.jpg/250px-GreenSt_plaque_1.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:GreenSt_plaque_1.jpg)

The plaque embedded in the pavement on Green Street in San Francisco

A series of letters written by Green are currently stored in the [Bancroft Library](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bancroft_Library "Bancroft Library") of the University of California.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talbot_H._Green#cite_note-FOOTNOTELarkin1850-75)

Green Street in San Francisco was named in honor of Talbot H. Green,[[j]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talbot_H._Green#cite_note-77) along with other streets named after California pioneers such as Larkin, Brannan, Folsom and Howard.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talbot_H._Green#cite_note-78)[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talbot_H._Green#cite_note-79) Green Street runs through several neighborhoods, including [North Beach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Beach,_San_Francisco "North Beach, San Francisco") and [Russian Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_Hill,_San_Francisco "Russian Hill, San Francisco"), which are areas rich in San Francisco's history.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talbot_H._Green#cite_note-80)

Where your donation goes

 Accountability and transparency are core values at the Wikimedia Foundation. We manage funds and resources to ensure that every contribution supports our mission. We have earned the Platinum Seal of Transparency from Candid (formerly GuideStar), and Charity Navigator awarded us its highest rating. You can [read our most recent annual report](https://wikimediafoundation.org/annualreports/current/) for more information about our financial health. 

45% Investment in Technology 
Nearly half of our budget goes toward supporting the technology that powers Wikipedia and other Wikimedia projects. We are constantly working to enhance the user experience for both contributors and readers, improve site security, and ensure reliable access to our websites globally. This infrastructure and product support sustain one of the top ten most visited websites in the world, all at a fraction of the cost of popular for-profit websites.

32% Support for Volunteers 
The global reach of Wikimedia projects is made possible by the hard work of volunteers from across the globe. We provide grants, legal support, and other resources to help build vibrant volunteer communities. Additionally, we promote community engagement through outreach initiatives and advocate for the growth and protection of free knowledge.

12% Allocation to Fundraising Efforts 
Donor support is crucial to sustaining Wikipedia and our other free knowledge endeavors. Our team is committed to efficient and effective fundraising throughout the year, ensuring that every contribution helps advance our mission.

11% General and Administrative Expenses 
Operational costs are essential for the smooth management and governance of the Wikimedia Foundation. These expenses help us recruit top talent and support staff around the world, empowering them to carry out the mission of the Wikimedia Foundation.

**Rita A. Crundwell** (née **Humphrey**; born January 10, 1953) is an American woman who served as the [comptroller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comptroller "Comptroller") and [treasurer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treasurer "Treasurer") of [Dixon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dixon,_Illinois "Dixon, Illinois"), [Illinois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illinois "Illinois"), from 1983 to 2012. She was fired and arrested in April 2012 after the discovery that she had [embezzled](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Embezzlement "Embezzlement") $53.7 million from the city of Dixon for over 22 years to support her championship [American Quarter Horse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Quarter_Horse "American Quarter Horse") breeding operation, as well as a lavish lifestyle away from work.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rita_Crundwell#cite_note-Chicago_Tribune_Jenco-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rita_Crundwell#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rita_Crundwell#cite_note-3) Her embezzlement has been described as the largest municipal fraud in U.S. history.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rita_Crundwell#cite_note-4) Crundwell pleaded guilty to her crimes and was sentenced to 19 years and 7 months in prison.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rita_Crundwell#cite_note-Forbes_sentencing-5)

Crundwell used the money to turn her Quarter Horse breeding operation, RC Quarter Horses, into one of the best-known in the country. Her horses won 52 world championships and she was named the leading owner by the [American Quarter Horse Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Quarter_Horse_Association "American Quarter Horse Association") for eight consecutive years prior to her arrest.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rita_Crundwell#cite_note-JencoGrimm-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rita_Crundwell#cite_note-Keyser-7) She spent 8+1⁄2 years (43% of her sentence) in prison before being released in mid-2021 to serve the remainder of her sentence in home confinement. Her sentence was [commuted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commutation_(law) "Commutation (law)") along with nearly 1500 other people by President Biden on December 12, 2024. Those commuted were people who had been previously transferred from prison to house arrest under the [CARES Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CARES_Act "CARES Act") due to having a high risk of COVID-19.

## Early life and career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rita_Crundwell&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and career")]

Born Rita Humphrey, the daughter of Ray and Caroline Humphrey,[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rita_Crundwell#cite_note-Giuliana-8) Crundwell grew up on her family's farm near Dixon,[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rita_Crundwell#cite_note-Keyser-7) and was a student at [Dixon High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dixon_High_School_(Illinois) "Dixon High School (Illinois)"). In 1970, a year before graduating,[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rita_Crundwell#cite_note-Keyser-7) the teenager began working at the Dixon City Hall as a work-study student.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rita_Crundwell#cite_note-Forbes_sentencing-5) She began showing [American Quarter Horses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Quarter_Horse "American Quarter Horse") in 1978.

She married engineering technician Jerry L. Crundwell in 1974, while working as a secretary for Dixon's mayor, but divorced Crundwell in 1986.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rita_Crundwell#cite_note-9)

In 1983, Crundwell was appointed the [treasurer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treasurer "Treasurer") and [comptroller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comptroller "Comptroller") for Dixon, working in this capacity for almost three decades.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rita_Crundwell#cite_note-Forbes_sentencing-5)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rita_Crundwell#cite_note-Keyser-7)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rita_Crundwell#cite_note-10) Crundwell acquired a sterling reputation; in 2011, one of the city commissioners praised her stewardship of city finances, saying that "she looks after every tax dollar as if it were her own."[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rita_Crundwell#cite_note-11)

## Embezzlement

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rita_Crundwell&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Embezzlement")]

In 1990, Crundwell opened a bank account named the Reserve Sewer Capital Development Account (RSCDA), making it appear to be a city account. She was the only [signatory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Signature "Signature"). Crundwell would have money deposited into another account called the Capital Development Fund, create false state [invoices](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Invoice "Invoice"), and then write checks from the fund payable to "Treasurer", which she would deposit into the RSCDA account. According to federal investigators, this relatively uncomplicated scheme continued for 22 years.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rita_Crundwell#cite_note-Forbes_sentencing-5)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rita_Crundwell#cite_note-AmericanGreed-12)

On average, Crundwell stole nearly $2.5 million per year from the city, starting from a low of $181,000 in 1991, growing to the embezzlement of $5.8 million in 2008–from a city with an annual budget of $8–9 million.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rita_Crundwell#cite_note-Forbes_sentencing-5)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rita_Crundwell#cite_note-13) Crundwell used the money not only to finance her Quarter Horse operation, but also to support a lifestyle well beyond her $80,000 city salary, purchasing several cars, a second house[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rita_Crundwell#cite_note-14) and a $2.1 million 45-foot luxury [motorhome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motorhome "Motorhome").[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rita_Crundwell#cite_note-15)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rita_Crundwell#cite_note-16)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rita_Crundwell#cite_note-17)

Crundwell covered up her [embezzlement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Embezzlement "Embezzlement") by claiming that the city's frequent budget shortfalls were due to the state being late in paying its share of [tax revenue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tax_revenue "Tax revenue").[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rita_Crundwell#cite_note-plea-18) She forced city departments to make drastic service cuts to keep the budget within reason. As a result, employees went two years or more without raises and the police department could not afford new radios.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rita_Crundwell#cite_note-19) The most visible effect, however, was on street maintenance; the city was forced to lay off three of its nine street repair workers and cut the rate of maintenance. In the decade before Crundwell's arrest, only 65 blocks of road were repaired or replaced.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rita_Crundwell#cite_note-appeal-20)

For most of Crundwell's tenure, residents assumed either that she inherited her wealth and/or that her horse breeding business was profitable in its own right. However, by the onset of the [Great Recession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Recession "Great Recession"), some grew suspicious that Crundwell was stealing money. But the city's outside [auditors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auditor "Auditor"), Clifton Gunderson (now [CliftonLarsonAllen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CliftonLarsonAllen "CliftonLarsonAllen") after merging with LarsonAllen in 2012) and local accountant Samuel Card presumed that Crundwell was honest and signed off on her annual financial statements without concern. For small U.S. cities similar to Dixon, lack of sufficient outside audits was a recurring problem, as third-party auditors could give at best limited attention. For most of her tenure as comptroller, Crundwell had nearly complete control over the city's accounts, while few city employees had access to the city's financial statements.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rita_Crundwell#cite_note-Forbes_sentencing-5)

## Capture and arrest

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rita_Crundwell&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Capture and arrest")]

In the fall of 2011, while Crundwell was on an extended vacation, city clerk and acting comptroller Kathe Swanson discovered the RSCDA account with 179 deposits and associated checking activity.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rita_Crundwell#cite_note-Keyser-7) Swanson did not recognize the account as a legitimate city account, and alerted Dixon [mayor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayor "Mayor") James Burke. In turn, Burke contacted the [Federal Bureau of Investigation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Bureau_of_Investigation "Federal Bureau of Investigation") (FBI). For the next six months, Burke and Swanson (whose payroll was controlled by Crundwell) remained silent while the FBI built their case.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rita_Crundwell#cite_note-AmericanGreed-12)

Crundwell arrived for work on April 17, 2012, to find FBI agents waiting for her. She was arrested later that day and was [indicted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indictment "Indictment") by a federal [grand jury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_jury "Grand jury") for embezzling $53 million in city money over the previous six years.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rita_Crundwell#cite_note-JencoGrimm-6)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rita_Crundwell#cite_note-AmericanGreed-12)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rita_Crundwell#cite_note-21) Crundwell was charged with one count of [wire fraud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mail_and_wire_fraud "Mail and wire fraud") and released on $4,500 [bail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bail "Bail") the next day.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rita_Crundwell#cite_note-22)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rita_Crundwell#cite_note-23) On May 2, 2012, a superseding indictment charged Crundwell with embezzling $53 million over the prior 22 years.

On November 14, 2012, Crundwell pleaded guilty before Judge [Philip Reinhard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_Godfrey_Reinhard "Philip Godfrey Reinhard") to a single count of wire fraud.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rita_Crundwell#cite_note-24) As part of the deal, she also admitted to [money laundering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Money_laundering "Money laundering") by using the embezzled money to finance her horse operation. Crundwell was required to forfeit more than $53.7 million in cash, assets and possessions, equivalent to the amount she stole, which is being used to make full [restitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Restitution "Restitution") to the city.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rita_Crundwell#cite_note-plea-18) She reportedly told FBI agents that some of the money was spent on her horses and their upkeep. [Prosecutors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prosecutor "Prosecutor") sought the [forfeiture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asset_forfeiture "Asset forfeiture") of her horse farm and 300 horses, in addition to her three homes and a luxury motorhome vehicle.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rita_Crundwell#cite_note-JencoGrimm-6) Prosecutors later discovered that Crundwell's crimes had begun as early as 1988, when she siphoned off $25,000 from the Dixon Sister City program over two years.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rita_Crundwell#cite_note-Chicago_Tribune_Jenco-1) Had she not pleaded guilty, she would have faced additional charges of [bank fraud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_fraud "Bank fraud"), wire fraud, and money laundering that could have sent her to prison for the rest of her life.

The following month, Dixon's new finance director said that the city had seen an almost $3 million rebound since Crundwell's arrest, but that the operating budget was still off by $16.6 million.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rita_Crundwell#cite_note-Peoria_Journal_Star_budget_rebounding-25) It was also reported that Dixon lost $30 million in operating funds over the prior decade.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rita_Crundwell#cite_note-Peoria_Journal_Star_budget_rebounding-25) The city sued its outside auditors, as well as the city's banker, [Fifth Third Bank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fifth_Third_Bank "Fifth Third Bank"), for ignoring numerous red flags in Crundwell's actions. In September 2013, the auditors and Fifth Third agreed to pay the city $40 million in a [legal settlement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Settlement_(litigation) "Settlement (litigation)"), while the auction of Crundwell's assets brought in over $9 million.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rita_Crundwell#cite_note-26) Richard Humphrey Jr., Crundwell's nephew, purchased the 88-acre (36 ha) horse ranch formerly owned by Crundwell, for $1 million in an auction a few days before she was sentenced.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rita_Crundwell#cite_note-27) Her brother, Richard, purchased one of the houses she owned in Dixon.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rita_Crundwell#cite_note-28) The property includes 40 acres (16 ha) of farmland that borders another 40 acres of farmland he owns.

At sentencing on February 14, 2013, prosecutors sought the maximum sentence of 20 years in federal prison. Their case was bolstered by testimony from Burke and city staffers that Crundwell used dramatic analogies to force spending cuts to cover up her theft, which left Dixon unable to provide the most basic services. The [defense](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Defense_(legal) "Defense (legal)") asked for 13 years, saying that Crundwell had cooperated with authorities in recovering the money. Ultimately, Reinhard sentenced Crundwell to 19 years and 7 months in prison, close to what prosecutors had sought. Reinhard noted that she put her passion for raising horses ahead of the needs of the city residents who had entrusted her with their funds, and that a significant prison term was required to restore public confidence. Reinhard was so disgusted with Crundwell's behavior that he revoked her bail and remanded her to custody rather than allow her to self-report to prison.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rita_Crundwell#cite_note-Forbes_sentencing-5)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rita_Crundwell#cite_note-Chicago_Tribune_Jenco-1)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rita_Crundwell#cite_note-appeal-20)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rita_Crundwell#cite_note-Peoria_Journal_Star_Babwin-29) Crundwell [appealed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Appeal "Appeal") the sentence, but the [Seventh Circuit Court of Appeals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Court_of_Appeals_for_the_Seventh_Circuit "United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit") upheld it in November 2013.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rita_Crundwell#cite_note-appeal-20)

Crundwell's embezzlement has been the subject of academic and professional publications.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rita_Crundwell#cite_note-30)

On September 20, 2012, Crundwell was also indicted on 60 state counts of theft, alleging that she stole $11.2 million from April 2010 until the day of her arrest. Burke and [Lee County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lee_County,_Illinois "Lee County, Illinois") State's Attorney Henry Dixon said the state charges, which carried a minimum of 6 years per count, were a backup in case Crundwell was [acquitted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acquittal "Acquittal") on the federal charges.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rita_Crundwell#cite_note-31) The state charges were dropped in April 2013. Dixon's successor as state's attorney, Anna Sacco-Miller, said that it did not make sense to spend taxpayer money on prosecuting Crundwell, as there were virtually no assets left for the state to seize (though Dixon had initially said he had no plans to seize assets from her). Sacco-Miller also said that because Illinois sentencing guidelines require state and federal sentences to run concurrently, Crundwell would likely serve out any sentence imposed at the state level while she was still in federal prison.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rita_Crundwell#cite_note-32)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rita_Crundwell#cite_note-33)

## Prison and release

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rita_Crundwell&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Prison and release")]

Crundwell was incarcerated at minimum-security [Federal Correctional Institution, Waseca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Correctional_Institution,_Waseca "Federal Correctional Institution, Waseca") in [Waseca, Minnesota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waseca,_Minnesota "Waseca, Minnesota"). She was originally eligible and scheduled for release after serving 85% of her sentence (16 years 8 months) on March 5, 2030.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rita_Crundwell#cite_note-34) Under the [First Step Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Step_Act "First Step Act") she was receiving [good conduct time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Good_conduct_time "Good conduct time") deductions of 54 days per year off her sentence.

On April 27, 2020, Crundwell submitted a request for a compassionate release with the warden of the Federal Prison Camp in Waseca. On that same date she filed a motion with the Illinois Northern District Court in Rockford, Illinois.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rita_Crundwell#cite_note-letter-35) Her motion requested home confinement under the First Step Act. The motion also sought a transfer to home confinement based on a [Response to the COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_on_prisons "Impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on prisons") memo dated March 26, 2020, from Attorney General [William Barr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Barr "William Barr") to the [Federal Bureau of Prisons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Bureau_of_Prisons "Federal Bureau of Prisons"). Crundwell cited, amongst other things, her "health issues, including high blood pressure and high cholesterol"[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rita_Crundwell#cite_note-letter-35)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rita_Crundwell#cite_note-downersgrove-36) and her good conduct while incarcerated. The motion was withdrawn by Crundwell on May 18, 2020, a few days after Dixon City Council strongly opposed an early release. The motion withdrawing the home confinement request was granted on May 21, 2020.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rita_Crundwell#cite_note-37)

A little over a year later, on August 4, 2021, after serving half of the required 45% of her sentence (about 8+1⁄2 years), she was released by the Federal Bureau of Prisons (i.e. not by a court) on compassionate grounds to a _residential reentry center_ - a [halfway house](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halfway_house "Halfway house")[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rita_Crundwell#cite_note-38) or a home confinement,[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rita_Crundwell#cite_note-39) possibly her brother, Richard Humphrey's ranch (farm[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rita_Crundwell#cite_note-letter-35)) in Dixon as she proposed in her previously withdrawn request for release.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rita_Crundwell#cite_note-houseconfinement-40) Two months later in October 2021, she was reported to live at the brother's 80-acre farm.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rita_Crundwell#cite_note-BackInDixon-41) Because she is serving her sentence in home confinement, she's not allowed to leave the farm property without permission. She was overseen by a residential reentry management field office in Chicago suburb [Downers Grove](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Downers_Grove,_Illinois "Downers Grove, Illinois").[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rita_Crundwell#cite_note-downersgrove-36)

On December 12, 2024, Crundwell's sentence was commuted by President [Joe Biden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden "Joe Biden") along with nearly 1500 other individuals who were previously released under the CARES Act, which allowed people with a high risk of COVID-19 to be released from prison into home detention.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rita_Crundwell#cite_note-m490-42)

Crundwell's story was featured on the January 15, 2025, edition of [Freeform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freeform_(TV_channel) "Freeform (TV channel)")'s _Scam Goddess_, hosted by [Laci Mosley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laci_Mosley "Laci Mosley").[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rita_Crundwell#cite_note-43)
